content:
5      POST-16
STUDENT TRANSPORT POLICY – MAINSTREAM EDUCATION 2026/27
– The Director Communities submitted a report seeking
approval for the Post-16 Student Transport Policy –
Mainstream Education for the 2026/27 academic year and for the
Council to enter into a Grant Offer Letter with participating
colleges and school sixth forms, setting out the terms and
conditions of the grant and the associated monitoring
arrangements.
 
The
proposed policy provided for a travel grant of £374.57 per
eligible student for learners of sixth form age attending
mainstream further education or school sixth form provision, where
they lived more than three miles from their place of study which is
an additional benefit to North Lincolnshire parents and not a
statutory requirement of the policy.
 
North Lincolnshire Council published annual post-16 transport
policy statements. This report was related to the mainstream
post-16 student transport policy for 2026/27. During the 2025/26
academic year, transport support was provided to 902 students who
lived more than three miles from their institution and travelled
between home and college or school sixth form provision during term
time.
 
Under Section 509AA of the Education Act 1996, the Council was
required to prepare and publish an annual transport policy
statement setting out the arrangements it considered necessary to
facilitate the attendance of people of sixth form age receiving
education or training. The statutory framework did not require
North Lincolnshire Council to provide free transport in all cases,
and parents and learners may be expected to make a contribution towards costs.
 
The
proposed arrangements were intended to support continued
participation in education and training, provide flexibility for
students and families, and promote the use of sustainable transport
wherever public transport was available.
 
A
Grant Offer Letter had been prepared for the Council, participating
colleges and school sixth forms. This set out the terms and
conditions of the grant, including the basis of payment, use of the
grant, and monitoring arrangements.
 
Resolved – That the Post 16
Student Transport Policy – Mainstream Education for the
2026/27 academic year, including a travel grant of £374.57
for each eligible student, be approved, and (b) that the proposal
for North Lincolnshire Council to enter
into and sign the Grant Offer Letter with participating
colleges and school sixth forms, be approved.
topline: The Children, Families and Young People Cabinet Member has decided to approve the Post-16 Student Transport Policy for the 2026/27 academic year, including a travel grant for eligible students.

1      CIVIL
PARKING ENFORCEMENT POLICY - REVISED 2026 – The Director:
Communities submitted a report seeking approval to the adoption of
a revised Civil Parking Enforcement Policy.
 
North Lincolnshire Council adopted Civil Parking Enforcement,
which allowed for council-led enforcement of parking restrictions
using civil penalties (PCNs) instead of criminal fines.
 
This
system was enabled under the Traffic Management Act 2004 and was
designed to ensure safer, free-flowing roads by enforcing on-street
parking restrictions.
 
Following the adoption of these powers, North Lincolnshire
Council operated under this policy to achieve its outcomes for
people and place, including maintaining safe and free-flowing
traffic, preventing dangerous parking, improving access to shops,
services and residential areas, and supporting wider transport and
place-based outcomes.
 
The
existing Civil Parking Enforcement Policy was reviewed and updated
to ensure that it continued to reflect best practice, providing
clear guidance to the public on how civil parking provisions would
be enforced within North Lincolnshire.
 
Resolved – That the adoption of
the revised Civil Parking Enforcement Policy, be
approved.

4     
RECONSTITUTION OF THE RIVERSIDE FEDERATION – The
Director: Children and Families submitted a report seeking approval
to consider the instrument of government to allow the governing
body of The Riverside Federation to be reconstituted with effect
from 1 July 2026.
 
At
the full governing body meeting of The Riverside Federation held on
26 March 2026, the governors voted to reconstitute the governing
body in line with the School Governance (Constitution) (England)
Regulations 2012 and the School Governance (Constitution)
(Amendment) Regulations 2014.
 
The
constitution of each governing body was set out in a document known
as the instrument of government. A governing body could, at any
time, request changes to its constitution, in accordance with the
regulations, by varying its instrument of government. Where changes
were proposed, a maintained school’s governing body was
required to prepare a draft instrument of government and submit it
to the local authority for approval.
 
If
the local authority is not content with the draft instrument of
government, it was required to advise the governing body and give
reasons. If it was not possible for the local authority and the
governing body to agree on a revised draft, the local authority
would produce a final draft for the school as it thought fit,
having regard to the category of school to which the school
belonged.
 
Resolved – That the new
instrument of government for The Riverside Federation, as set out
in the report, be approved.

decision_maker: Children, Families and Young People Cabinet Member
content:
2        FOSTERING
ALLOWANCE RATES 2026-27 – The Director: Children and
Families submitted a report seeking approval to increase the
allowance rate paid to foster carers in line with the
Government’s recent announcement to raise the National
Minimum Allowance.
 
North Lincolnshire Council had a long-standing record of
ensuring children in care lived locally in high-quality foster care
families. At that time, 83% children in foster care lived with
North Lincolnshire Council approved foster carers (including
kinship foster carers), which was significantly higher than in many
other local authorities that had relied more heavily on independent
fostering agencies and eternal residential homes.
 
Foster carers in North Lincolnshire had benefited from excellent
support, with the Council investing in effective recruitment and
marketing activity. The North Lincolnshire ‘offer’ had
become more important than ever, given the increasing local
presence of independent providers seeking to compete for new foster
carers and to persuade existing fostering households to
transfer.
 
The
Care Standards Act 2000 had set out the Fostering National Minimum
Standards, which Fostering Services and foster carers were required
to adhere to. A key element of this had been the principle that
foster carers should not be financially disadvantaged through
undertaking their role.
 
North Lincolnshire had honoured the National Fostering Minimum
Allowance, in many cases paying above these rates, and had offered
where appropriate, enhanced financial packages based on the
specific needs of children and in recognition of foster carer
skills and experience. This, alongside the high levels of support
from the fostering team and the family-focused culture of North
Lincolnshire Council helps to retain foster carers in an
increasingly competitive market.
 
In
January 2026, the Government had announced an increase of 3.35% for
the 2026/27 Fostering Minimum Allowance. The Government had stated
that this was in line with inflation and Local Government
affordability; any increase in rates should not have impacted upon
other financial support already in place.
 
Resolved – That the increase in
Foster Care allowances, as set out in the report, be
approved.
topline: The Children, Families and Young People Cabinet Member has decided to increase foster care allowance rates in North Lincolnshire

decision_maker: Children, Families and Young People Cabinet Member
content:
3        SUPPORTED
LODGING PROVIDER RATES 2026-27 – The Director: Children
and Families submitted a report seeking approval to increase the
allowance rate paid to Supported Lodging Providers for 2026-27, in
order to align North Lincolnshire Council rates with those of
neighbouring authorities and ensure that the local offer for
providers was competitive.
 
North Lincolnshire Council had a long-standing record of helping
to ensure children lived with their families and in kinship
arrangements. For those who had needed to enter the care of the
local authority, remaining close to home had been an absolute
priority, which was why continued efforts to retain supported
lodgings providers had been essential.
 
At
that time, there were very few children and young people living in
supported lodgings households, however
these arrangements had often been the best way for older children
in care and care leavers to receive support whilst developing
independence skills. Recruiting more supported lodgings providers
had been identified as an important area of development within the
Sufficiency Strategy.
 
Unlike with foster carers, supported lodgings provider rates had
not been subject to government minimum allowance recommendations.
In North Lincolnshire, the weekly rates had not been increased for
three years and, as a result, the rates had fallen below those paid
by neighbouring local authorities.
 
Resolved – That the percentage
uplift to the Supported Lodging allowance, bringing weekly rates in
line with those of neighbouring local authorities, as set out in
the report, be approved.
topline: The Children, Families and Young People Cabinet Member has decided to increase the allowance rate for Supported Lodging Providers for 2026-27.

9      
NEW PLANNING VALIDATION CHECKLIST AND NEW PREAPPLICATION ADVICE
REQUEST PROCESS – The Director: Communities submitted a
report seeking approval for the public consultation to be carried
out on the new validation planning checklist 2026 and updating on
the changes to the pre application advice service schedule
2026.
 
The
previous validation checklist was designed as an interim checklist
in 2018. The new validation checklist was updated to reflect
relevant national and local validation requirements for planning
applications, including the new Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG)
mandatory requirements.
 
The
proposed validation checklist was redesigned with a clearer and
easier to read layout, with each section set out in paragraph
format, rather than table format. The final draft version of the
proposed validation checklist was presented to external planning
agents at a recent North Lincolnshire Planning Agent’s Forum,
where agents indicated that they preferred the layout and
formatting of the proposed validation checklist.
 
The
previous pre-application advice service, which also included
permitted development enquiries, was originally published in 2021.
The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) encouraged early
engagement in the form of pre-application advice, as this had
significant potential to improve the efficiency and effectiveness
of the planning application system for all parties. Good quality
pre-application discussions enabled better coordination between
public and private resources and improved outcomes for the
community.
 
Local planning authorities played a key role in encouraging
other parties to take maximum advantage of the pre-application
stage. The more issues that were resolved at the pre-application
stage, including the need to deliver improvements in infrastructure
and affordable housing, the greater the benefits to North
Lincolnshire.
 
Following discussions with external planning agents and feedback
from the public, it was found that their requirements and
expectations of the preapplication service were not being met. This
resulted in customers and stakeholders being hesitant to use the
existing pre-application service.
 
The
updated pre-application advice service schedule was structured as a
two-tier approach, as set out in the report.
 
Resolved – (a) That the new
validation checklist for public consultation, be approved. and (b)
the updated pre application advice service schedule is noted, be
approved.

8      REWET,
REWILD, RECONNECT - RIPARIAN REVIVAL IN NORTH LINCOLNSHIRE PROJECT
– The Director: Communities submitted a report seeking
approval for the distribution of a community questionnaire to
determine local appetite for progressing the Rewet, Rewild,
Reconnect: Riparian Revival for North Lincolnshire
project.
 
North Lincolnshire had experienced significant historic
alteration and loss of watercourses, ponds and riparian corridors,
resulting in reduced biodiversity, increased flood risk and a
weakening of community connection to local landscapes.
 
The
council through the Strategic Flood Risk Team, had been exploring
the potential for a place-based riparian restoration and community
engagement project that would address these issues through
nature-based solutions, education and volunteering, delivered with
external funding support.
 
The
proposed project at Barton upon Humber had been developed to an
early, exploratory stage. A literature review had already been
completed, evidencing the environmental, flood risk and social
benefits of riparian restoration. Barton upon Humber Town Council
had also expressed support in principle and a desire for the
project to be explored further within its area.
 
Before any decision was taken to progress the project, it was
essential that the council established whether there was a genuine
community interest and support. The questionnaire provided a
proportionate and transparent mechanism for residents to express
their views on riparian restoration, accessibility, education,
heritage and community involvement.
 
The
questionnaire formed one of three key pieces of evidence required
to demonstrate need, demand and community alignment. The three
components were the completed literature review, formal support
from Barton Town Council, and feedback from residents and local
stakeholders obtained through the questionnaire. Collectively,
these provided a balanced evidence base combining academic
research, local democratic endorsement and direct community
input.
 
Should the questionnaire demonstrate clear community support,
the council would be in a position to consider progressing to the
next stage, as set out in the report.
 
Resolved – That distribution of
the community questionnaire to determine local appetite for
progressing the Rewet, Rewild, Reconnect: Riparian Revival for
North Lincolnshire project, be approved.
topline: The Environment and Strategy Cabinet Member has decided to distribute a community questionnaire to gauge local interest in a riparian restoration project in North Lincolnshire.

2     
TERMINAL ILLNESS COUNCIL TAX DISCOUNT SCHEME – The
Director: Transformation and Outcomes submitted a report seeking
approval for the introduction of a Terminal Illness Council Tax
Discount Scheme, providing 100% discretionary reduction in Council
Tax liability for eligible households experiencing severe financial
hardship as a result of terminal illness.
 
Households affected by terminal illness often experienced
significant additional costs alongside a reduction or loss of
household income. These pressures could create immediate and severe
financial hardship, including difficulty meeting Council Tax
liabilities at a time of acute emotional distress. 
 
While statutory Council Tax exemptions, discounts and Council
Tax Support (CTS) provided assistance, they did not always fully
mitigate the financial impact associated with terminal illness,
particularly where households fell outside CTS eligibility or
experienced sudden changes in circumstances. This had been
highlighted nationally as part of the Marie Curie Cost of Dying
Campaign which aimed to ensure no one faced poverty at the end of
life. The campaign encouraged the use of discretionary Council Tax
powers to support and protect terminally ill residents from
financial hardship.
 
The
Council had authority under Section 13A(1)(c) of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 to reduce Council Tax liability to any
extent, including 100%. The report proposed the use of that
discretion to introduce a targeted, compassionate scheme that fully
removed Council Tax liability for eligible households for a defined
period
 
The
scheme was proposed to operate from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2028,
with costs and take up monitored annually.
 
Resolved – (a) That the
introduction of the Terminal Illness Council Tax Discount Scheme,
with effect from 1 April 2026, be approved; (b) that the proposal
that the scheme be operated under Section 13A(1)(c) of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992, be approved, and (c) that authority to
make minor operational amendments to the scheme where required be
delegated to the Section 151 Officer, in consultation with the
relevant Portfolio Holder.
topline: The Independent Families - Adults and Health Cabinet Member has decided to introduce a Terminal Illness Council Tax Discount Scheme to provide support to eligible households facing severe financial hardship due to terminal illness.

3        WORK
EXPERIENCE POLICY – The Director: Transformation and
Outcomes submitted a report to outline and seek approval for a new
Work Experience policy, which aimed to support managers with
hosting short-term placements.
 
Currently, short-term work experience placements, such as those
available to school students, were managed within individual
services and usually arose from an ad-hoc enquiry.
 
‘Investing in People' was one of the three areas of focus
of the council's commitment to its workforce in the Organisational
Development plan and there was intent to develop the
council’s work experience offer, particularly to support
young people.
 
The
policy aligned with the Government’s Youth Guarantee, which
provided an entitlement to two weeks of work experience for young
people during school or college, as well as funding to help those
on Universal Credit develop job skills.
 
The
council was delivering Connect to Work: a locally-led, Government-funded programme designed to
help people with disability, health conditions and other complex
barriers to employment to get into, and stay in, work. Supporting
managers would host meaningful work experience placements which
would also potentially contribute to delivery of this
programme.
 
Approval was sought for a new Work Experience policy and
Placement Guide appendix. It intended that the policy and guide
would provide a consistent framework for managers across the
council and it gave them support and confidence in offering work
experience placements, particularly around planning and
induction.
 
The
policy was aimed at providing guidance to managers with short-term
work experience placements. The report gave details of the policy
and the Placement Guide which was appended to the
report.
 
Resolved – That the Work
Experience policy and Placement Guide appendix be
approved.

6        LOCAL
GOVERNMENT REORGANISATION (LGR) IN GREATER LINCOLNSHIRE STATUTORY
CONSULTATION RESPONSE - The Chief Executive submitted an urgent
report seeking approval to submit a response to Ministry of
Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) statutory
consultation on Local Government Reorganisation in Greater
Lincolnshire and to delegate authority to the Chief Executive to
submit the council’s response prior to the close of the
statutory consultation.
 
On 5
February 2025, the Secretary of State wrote to the Leaders of North
Lincolnshire Council, Lincolnshire County Council; the City,
District and Borough Councils; and North East Lincolnshire Council,
formally inviting them to submit proposals for a single tier of
local government for the area.
 
The
council’s proposal was one of four proposals submitted across
Greater Lincolnshire. The four proposals were subject to statutory
consultation by MHCLG. Statutory consultation was a national
process led by the Secretary of State.
 
The
statutory consultation asked for feedback on the four proposals
submitted by Greater Lincolnshire Authorities. The report set out
details of the four proposals submitted by Greater Lincolnshire
Authorities.
 
Once
the consultation had been concluded the next steps would be for a
ministerial decision to be taken on whether to implement a proposal
(with or without modification); preparation and approval of
secondary legislation; and a transition period leading to vesting
day for any new authorities.
 
Therefore, an urgent decision is requested as the council as
must respond to the Government Statutory Consultation by 23:59 on
26 March 2026.
 
Resolved – (a) That the
statutory consultation process for Local Government Reorganisation
in Greater Lincolnshire be noted; (b) that the proposed responses
to the MHCLG statutory consultation questions, including the
explicit support for North Lincolnshire Councils proposal (proposal
3) which was submitted to Government in November 2025, following
endorsement by Full Council on 25 November 2025, be approved, and
(c) that authority be delegated to the Chief Executive to submit
the response to MHCLG, including any minor changes, prior to the
close of the statutory consultation.

5         
SECTION 101 AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GREATER LINCOLNSHIRE COMBINED
COUNTY AUTHORITY AND THE CONSTITUENT AUTHORITIES– The
Director: Communities submitted an urgent report seeking approval
for the proposed delegation of transport functions from the Greater
Lincolnshire Combined County Authority (GLCCA) to the three
constituent authorities within Greater Lincolnshire.
 
The
Greater Lincolnshire Combined County Authority (GLCCA) would become
the Local Transport Authority (LTA) for the Greater Lincolnshire
area and take on the associated responsibilities and local public
transport powers on 1 April 2026. These functions included
transport strategy, planning investment, delivering investment and
operations and maintenance across Rail, Road and Bus
networks.
 
The
Greater Lincolnshire Combined Authority Regulations 2025 (the
Regulations) stated that following the creation of the GLCCA in
March 2025, the majority of the functions relating to public
transport delivery would be held concurrently by the GLCCA and
constituent authorities during the transition period until 31 March
2026. Following the transition period, the majority of functions
were held solely by the GLCCA, which then had the duty to deliver
those functions.
 
Initially, with regards to transport, the GLCCA was established
as a commissioning and assurance organisation, with delivery being
undertaken by the Constituent Authorities in areas such as highways
authority and education travel.
 
The
principles of the Transport Transition Programme had been developed
and were agreed at the meeting of the GLCCA Transport Board on 12
November 2025. It was further agreed that the GLCCA would delegate
the powers for the following delivery areas to the constituent
authorities for a minimum period of 12 months commencing 1 April
2026: Transport Scheme Delivery and Operations and
Maintenance.
 
The
report set out further details of how the delegation of transport
functions would take place.
 
A urgent
decision had been requested in order to allow the statutory
timeframes to be met, as the agreement must be signed prior to 1
April 2026, when the powers would transfer to the Greater
Lincolnshire Combined County Authority.
 
Resolved – (a) That the
delegation of functions from the Greater Lincolnshire Combined
County Authority, in relation to transport functions as set out in
the regulations, be accepted, and (b) that the agreement and
signing of the S101 Agreement be delegated to the Chief Executive,
in consultation with the Leader of the Council.
topline: The Leader Portfolio for Community Leadership, Skills, Steel and Heavy Industry has decided to delegate transport functions from the Greater Lincolnshire Combined County Authority to the constituent authorities.

5         
ENVIRONMENT AGENCY BARTON UPON HUMBER TO NEW HOLLAND TIDAL FLOOD
ALLEVIATION SCHEME – FUNDING CONTRIBUTION FROM NORTH
LINCOLNSHIRE COUNCIL – The Director: Communities
submitted a report seeking approval to provide a funding
contribution to the Environment Agency to deliver the Barton upon
Humber – New Holland Tidal Flood Alleviation
Scheme.
 
The
Barton to New Holland Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme was proposed
to strengthen the existing defences along the frontage between the
Humber Bridge and the wharf at New Holland in areas where the most
residential and commercial properties were at risk. The initial
£0.5m contribution requested would cover works at Barrow
Haven using Property Flood Resilience measures and if funding
remained, prioritised repairs to the Barrow Haven flood
embankments. Following confirmation that the project was proceeding
to detailed design and construction phase, the additional
£0.5m would be to enable more resilience measures being
incorporated into the proposed Humber defences improvements
(although the details and costs of such measures were yet to be
determined, they would include installing secondary flood
resilience structures at New Holland Drain and Foster’s Wharf
outfall and additional flood resilience measures).
 
Post
the Project Steering Group Meeting and subsequent site meeting at
Barrow Haven the Environment Agency sent a letter to the Cabinet
Member for Operations and Flooding requesting a funding
contribution from North Lincolnshire Council to enhance the above
project and increase its scope. A total contribution of £1m
would enable more resilience measures to be incorporated more
swiftly and increase the confidence to unlock the Government
investment required, to deliver the project currently estimated at
£38.6m. The £1m contribution would be funded by the
council’s additional Highways and Flooding projects capital
fund.
 
The
report contained further information on The Barrow Haven Property
Flood Resilience Measures, Humber Defences Resilience Measures,
In-Kind Benefits and Reformed Defra Funding Policy.
 
Resolved – That Option 1, as set
out in the report at paragraph 3.1, be approved.

within the Trent Vale Area Action Plan. It supported an
infrastructure-first approach by improving traffic distribution,
enabling early housing delivery and strengthening the
council’s ability to secure Section 106 contributions for
wider infrastructure.
 
The
estimated cost of the scheme was £3.9m. To accelerate
delivery, it was proposed that the council provides an Onward Grant
to Keepmoat Homes, allowing the infrastructure to be delivered to
support improvements in the local road network for local residents
by completing the Burringham Bypass and
deliver housing growth.

and (b) that authority be delegated to Director: Communities (in
consultation with the Section 151 Officer and Monitoring Officer)
to agree final terms, make minor amendments and complete all
documentation, and to take all operational decisions to implement

content:
4        NORTH
LINCOLNSHIRE COUNCIL NON-IMMEDIATE ARTICLE 4 DIRECTION CONSULTATION
UPDATE AND CONFIRMATION – The Director: Communities
submitted a report informing the Cabinet Member about North
Lincolnshire Council Non-Immediate Article 4 Public Consultation
feedback and confirming the Non-Immediate Article 4 Direction for
the Town of Scunthorpe.
 
An
article 4 Directive restricted permitted development rights for
specific properties or areas and for North Lincolnshire this would
be to in relation to Houses In Multiple Occupation (HMOs). This
would require planning applications to be submitted for such
proposals to enable full and proper consideration of the potential
impacts of a proposed HMO on local amenity and the surrounding
community prior to the grant of planning permission.
 
Under national planning legislation, converting a property from
a single dwelling (Use Class C3) to a small HMO (Use Class C4)
currently fell under permitted development rights, meaning no
planning permission was required.
 
The
direction only applied to the conversion of ‘small
HMOs’, which had between three and six unrelated occupiers.
‘Large HMOs’, which were occupied by more than six
unrelated occupiers, were already subject to planning
permission.
 
Cabinet previously approved an action plan to undertake public
consultation to support the introduction of a
non?immediate Article 4
Direction restricted permitted development rights for changes of
use from C3 to C4 within Scunthorpe.
 
A
public consultation on the introduction of the Article 4 Direction
was undertaken between 27 November 2025 to 31 December 2025. The
consultation sought comments on the intention to introduce an
Article 4 Direction to remove permitted development rights for the
change of use from Use Class C3 (dwelling houses) to Use Class C4
(small houses in multiple occupation) across the whole of
Scunthorpe. Seventy-Two responses were received, the majority of respondents supported the
intention to introduce the Article 4 Direction. A more detailed
breakdown of the consultation responses was set out in the
appendices to the report.
 
The
report set out details of the consultation and of the next steps to
be taken.
 
Resolved – (a) That the contents
of the report and appendices be noted, and (b) that the proposal to
confirm the Non-Immediate Article 4 Direction for Scunthorpe, be
approved.

6         
SCHOOL ADMISSION ARRANGEMENTS FOR 2027/28 COMMUNITY AND
VOLUNTARY CONTROLLED SCHOOLS – The Director: Children and
Families submitted a report informing the Cabinet Member of the
outcome of the consultation with schools in respect of admission
arrangements for 2027/28, and seeking
approval to implement the proposed admission arrangements for the
2027/28 academic year.
 
The
council was required to determine by 28 February 2026 its admission
arrangements for the academic year 2027/28, including admission
numbers, for each community and voluntary controlled
school.
 
Admission arrangements were to describe how school places were
allocated, especially with reference to the oversubscription
criteria.  This confirmed how
applications were prioritised when the number of applications
exceeded the number of places available.
 
The
admission number referred to the number of places that the
admission authority must offer in the relevant age group of the
school. 
 
The
School Admissions Code 2021 required that oversubscription criteria
must be reasonable, clear, objective, procedurally fair, and
complied with all relevant legislation, including equalities
legislation.
 
A
full public consultation was carried out for the 2027/28
arrangements.
 
The
council consulted with each school governing board during the
Autumn Term 2025. The governing boards supported the admission
arrangements and all but five supported the proposed admission
number for their school.
 
Five
primary schools requested that their admission number be reduced.
Their proposals were discussed at the School Organisational Needs
Group (SONG). The group studied pupil projections for the planning
areas and planned housing developments and decided that the data
was not strong enough for reductions to be agreed for two of the
schools. Those schools’ admission numbers were therefore
unchanged in the arrangements from the previous year. There were no
officer objections to the other three schools reducing their
admission numbers, so they were put forward for public
consultation, as required by the School Admissions Code.
 
The
admissions numbers for the schools were publicly consulted on
between 17 December 2025 and 30 January 2026.
 
Resolved – That the proposed
admission numbers, admission arrangements and coordinated admission
schemes for the 2027/28 academic year, as set out in Appendix 1 to
the report, be approved.

their statutory duties. The regulations stipulated the categories
and number of governors for maintained schools.

 

Resolved – That

Federation be approved.

The
Director:  Children and Families
submitted a report updating the Cabinet Member on the 2026-27
funding allocations for Dedicated Schools Grant and the amount
available for Individual School Budgets and Early Years
providers.
 
The
Education and Skills Funding Agency (ESFA) published operational
guides annually to help local authorities and their Schools Forum
plan the local implementation of school funding formulas and
deliver early years entitlements for the forthcoming
year.
 
On
17 December 2025 the ESFA published the 2026-27 Dedicated Schools
Grant (DSG) Allocations, based on October 2025 School Census data.
The total allocation for North Lincolnshire was £212.246m
(£208.779 after recoupment and deductions for National
Non-Domestic Rates (NNDR) and direct funding of High Needs Places
by the Education and Skills Funding Agency (ESFA)). This was an
increase of £10.876m from last year, but includes the rolling
in of separate grants from 2025-26. The DSG consists of four
funding blocks.
 
The
schools block funded all mainstream schools and was ring fenced.
The Operational guide set out how Individual School Budget (ISB)
shares could be calculated.
 
The
council’s local school funding formula mirrored the schools
National Funding Formula (NFF). Key changes to the schools NFF in
2026 to 2027 affecting North Lincolnshire mainstream schools were
detailed in paragraph 2.5 of the report.
 
The
Early Years Block funded all providers of early education, early
years’ entitlements and key changes to the Early Years
Funding for 2026/27 were set out in the report at paragraphs 2.7,
2.8 and 2.9.
 
Local authorities determined their own local early years formula
that met the requirements of statutory guidance. Any changes to the
funding formulae must be in consultation with Schools Forum,
maintained schools and early years providers. 
 
The
report sets out the final proposals for the North Lincolnshire
Schools Funding Formula and the North Lincolnshire Early Years
Formula for 2026-27.

The
Director:  Children and Families
submitted a report seeking approval for the instrument of
government to allow the governing body of Crosby Primary School to
be reconstituted, to be effective from 1 January 2026.
 
At
the full governing body meeting of Crosby Primary School held on 4
November 2025, the governors voted to reconstitute the governing
body in line with the School Governance (Constitution) (England)
Regulations 2012 and the School Governance (Constitution)
(Amendment) Regulations 2014.
 
The
above regulations set out the options available to schools in terms
of the overall number of governors, the categories of governor and
the guiding principles for the constitution. The regulations gave
the governing body more flexibility with their constitution and
stated that they should be no bigger than they need to be to carry
out their statutory duties. The regulations stipulate the
categories and number of governors for maintained schools as
follows:
 
·      
2 parent governors (minimum)
 
·      
1 Local Authority governor (maximum)
 
·      
1 staff governor (maximum)
 
·      
1 Headteacher
 
·      
As many co-opted governors as necessary to fulfil
the skills requirements. Up to a maximum of one third of governors
can be staff members
 
The
constitution of each governing body was laid down in a document
known as the instrument of government. A governing body may at any
time request changes to their constitution, in accordance with the
regulations, by varying their instrument of government.
 
Where changes were proposed, a maintained school’s
governing body must prepare a draft instrument of government and
submit it to the local authority for approval.
 
Appendix 1 to the report set out the constitution of the
governing body in the form of an instrument of government, as
requested by the governors of Crosby Primary School.
 
Resolved – That the new
instrument of government for Crosby Primary School, as set out in
Appendix 1 to the report, be approved.
topline: The Independent Families - Children Cabinet Member has decided to approve the reconstitution of the governing body of Crosby Primary School.

2        NATIONAL
NON-DOMESTIC RATE DISCRETIONARY RELIEF APPLICATIONS – The
Director: Transformation and Outcomes submitted a report seeking a
decision on the level of National Non-Domestic Rate (NNDR)
discretionary relief to be awarded to eligible ratepayers in North
Lincolnshire.
 
The
arrangements for the collection of NNDR were set nationally through
legislation.  The legislation made
provision for councils to grant relief to a range of non-domestic
properties in a range of defined circumstances.  This included, for example, small business relief,
charitable relief and empty property relief.  Some relief was mandated and must be granted;
other relief was discretionary.  The
council also had a Hardship Relief scheme for cases of exceptional
hardship.
 
The
application of these provisions for granting NNDR relief helped
enable the council to deliver its council plan, specifically the
priorities of enabling economic growth and renewal enabling
resilient and flourishing communities.
 
Under the current regime of part localisation of NNDR, the
council funded a proportion of both mandatory and discretionary
reliefs it gave.
 
The
report considered two new applications for relief and set out the
proposed level based on an evaluation against set
criteria.
 
Resolved –That the level of rate
relief to each applicant, as set out in the appendix to the report,
be awarded.

2       
REGISTRATION FOR EMPLOYER SUPPORTED POLICING SCHEME –
The Director: Transformation and Outcomes submitted a report giving
an overview of the Employer Supported Policing Scheme and seeking
approval for the council to register to join the scheme.
 
Employer Supported Policing was a national scheme owned by the
Home Office. It was a partnership benefiting employers, their staff
and the police service by releasing Special Constables and Police
Support Volunteers to volunteer in the communities they
served.
 
The
scheme required employers to support employees who were, or would
like to become, a Special Constable or Police Support Volunteer by
allowing them some paid leave to undertake their duties or
training. The scheme did not specify a minimum or maximum amount of
paid leave that should be given, it was whatever was deemed
acceptable to the employer.
 
Benefits of registering for the scheme included:
 
·      
Demonstrating support for council employees and the
local community.
·      
Contributing to the council’s social
responsibility objectives.
·      
Enhancing the council’s reputation and profile
within the local community and as an employer.
·      
Facilitating employees to volunteer in a role which
offers transferable training and skills.
·      
Increasing reassurance to the community through more
visible policing.
·      
Providing police forces with greater resources for
reducing crime.
 
The
report gave details of how to register to join the scheme and how
it would work in practice.
 
Resolved – That the proposal to
register to join the Employer Supported Policing Scheme be
approved.

FEEDBACK ANNUAL REPORT – The Director: Transformation and
Outcomes submitted a report presenting the Customer Feedback Annual
Report 2024-25 – How Did We Do?
 
The
report presented a summary of the customer feedback received during
the period 1 April 2024 - 31 March 2025. Detailed findings were set
out in the accompanying appendix: Customer Feedback Annual Report
2023-24 – How Did We Do?
 
The
report’s purpose was to support the continuous improvement of
the council’s offer to residents and ensure that the learning
from customer feedback was captured and used to inform and enhance
customer experience moving forward. The annual report was therefore
important; it provided key intelligence and insight on how the
council was performing against published customer service standards
and as such, it was essential for informing the council’s
performance management, business assurance and public engagement
objectives.
 
There was a statutory requirement to present an annual report on
representations and complaints which had been addressed by adults
and children’s services through their respective regulated
processes. The initial stage of the complaints process rested with
the council where the principles of timely restorative practice
were applied. Subsequent stages required referral to the Local
Government and Social Care Ombudsman for independent
investigation.
 
The
report and appendix set out details of complaints received, along
with issues and findings.
 
Resolved – That the Customer
Feedback Annual Report 2024-25 – How Did We Do? be received
and approved for publication.

7        REVIEW OF
THE OLD CROSBY CONSERVATION AREA DESIGNATION – The
Director: Communities submitted a report seeking approval to begin
a consultation on the future status of the Old Crosby Conservation
area designation, and also to commence consultation on the
implementation of an Article 4(2) Direction, removing certain
permitted development rights.
 
Conservation areas should be of special architectural or
historic interest, the character or appearance of which it was
desirable to preserve or enhance. The preservation or enhancement
of conservation areas was secured via planning control and governed
by Section 72 Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas)
Act 1990. Where applications are required, the council “must
pay special attention to the desirability of preserving or
enhancing the character or appearance” of conservation
areas.
 
The
council had a duty to review conservation areas and amend them as
required under Section 69 Planning (Listed Buildings and
Conservation Areas) Act 1990. Old Crosby Conservation Area was
first designated in 1976, and the last review of the conservation
area was completed in 2002.
 
A
re-appraisal of the current Old Crosby conservation area had
recently been conducted. The review concluded that much of the
architectural interest and integrity that would result in the area
being classified as of “special interest” had been
lost. This was through alterations to properties, some of which may
have existed when the area was designated or were legal, permitted
development that was not subject to planning control nor could not
be controlled through planning enforcement as conservation area
status alone did not provide this. The adoption of an Article 4
Direction alongside the conservation area would have provided
greater protection, and an Article 4 Direction was required to
bring permitted development rights enjoyed in the conservation area
under planning control.
 
In
North Lincolnshire 12 of the 17 conservation areas have Article
4’s (some of which offered only partial coverage) and
generally it was noticeable that the areas without an associated
Article 4 were noticeably affected by damaging unsympathetic
development.
 
Approval was sought to commence a consultation exercise which
proposed to remove areas of the conservation area from the
designation that had lost this special character but retain the
historic core of the village of Old Crosby prior to its
incorporation into Scunthorpe as the town expanded.  The report set out the proposed new
boundary.
 
Resolved – That Option 1, as set
out the report at paragraph 3.1, be approved.
topline: The Environment and Strategy Cabinet Member has decided to review the Old Crosby Conservation Area designation and implement an Article 4(2) Direction to remove certain permitted development rights.

11     
KILLINGHOLME PRIMARY SCHOOL – PROPOSAL TO ESTABLISH A
MAINSTREAM SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS (SEN) STUDY HUB –
The Director: Children and Families submitted a report providing a
summary of responses to the formal consultation to establish a
mainstream SEN Study Hub at Killingholme Primary School, and
seeking approval for the proposal.
 
A
significant period of growth in Special Educational Needs and
Disabilities (SEND), both locally and nationally, had meant that
the council needed to identify further ways to meet its statutory
duty to ensure a sufficient number of places for children and young
people with SEND. The council’s strategic position was that
children and young people should, wherever possible, be educated in
their local communities.
 
The
proposal to establish a mainstream Study Hub in Killingholme
Primary School would provide children within key stage 1 and 2 with
additional needs, who currently may not need an Education, Health
or Care Plan or a specialist placement, access to a provision to
meet their specific needs.  Some pupils
did not require a specialist provision but may require a type of
education different to that of a standard mainstream school, always
with a view to return to their substantive classes or to their home
base within another local school.
 
The
Study Hub would provide an opportunity for a number of children
within the school and through consultation and referral from other
schools and the council to access to support and
learning.
 
Killingholme Primary School currently had a published admission
number (PAN) capacity of 126.  Once the
proposed changes had been implemented the PAN capacity would remain
at 126 mainstream places, 26 place nursery with the addition of up
to 10 council commissioned places within a formalised Study
Hub.
 
Under the Department for Education (DfE) statutory guidance for
making significant changes (‘prescribed alterations’)
to maintained schools, the council was the decision maker for
community schools.  Adding an SEN
provision to a mainstream school was deemed a significant
change.  The DfE guidance was followed
to publish a statutory notice with a period of four weeks for
representation (formal consultation). 
 
The
council either determined the proposal within two months of the end
of the consultation period or the decision fell to the Schools
Adjudicator.  Following publication of
the decision there was a four week ‘right of referral’
where the Diocesan Board of Education of the Church of England and
Roman Catholic Church may refer a decision made by the council to
the Schools Adjudicator.
 
Resolved – That the proposal to
establish a mainstream SEN Study Hub, as set out in paragraph 3.1
to the report, be approved.
topline: The Independent Families - Children Cabinet Member has decided to approve the establishment of a mainstream SEN Study Hub at Killingholme Primary School.

2        PROPOSAL FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT
REORGANISATION (LGR) IN GREATER LINCOLNSHIRE – The Chief
Executive submitted a report seeking approval to submit a proposal
for Local Government Reorganisation in Greater Lincolnshire by the
28 November 2025 deadline.  The proposal
recommended maintaining separate single Unitary Authorities for
North Lincolnshire and North East Lincolnshire, and converting
Lincolnshire County Council along with the districts into a single
Unitary Authority.
 
On
16 December 2024, the Government published the ‘English
Devolution White Paper’, setting out its ambitions to reform
public services across England by:
 
·      
Widening and broadening devolution across England
through the creation of new ‘Strategic Authorities’
and,
 
·      
Delivering a programme of local government
reorganisation to create new unitary councils across 21 county
areas.
 
The
White Paper outlined the Government’s intention to work at
pace with an ambitious timeframe for the delivery of both
devolution and local government reorganisation across the country.
As Lincolnshire had already achieved an ambitious devolution deal
the report concentrated on the aspects of the white paper in
relation to local government reorganisation.
 
On 5
February 2025 the Secretary of State wrote to the Leaders of North
Lincolnshire Council, Lincolnshire County Council, the City,
District and Borough Councils and North East Lincolnshire Council,
formally inviting them to submit proposals for a single tier of
local government for the area.  The
letter set out the statutory basis for the invitation and the
criteria against which proposals would be considered.
 
On
the 21 March 2025 North Lincolnshire Council, North East
Lincolnshire Council and Lincolnshire County Council submitted an
interim plan for LGR covering Greater Lincolnshire, as supported by
Full Council at an Extraordinary Meeting held on 18 March 2025
(minute 3061 refers).
 
Since submission of the interim plan work had continued to
develop a proposal for a single tier of local government across
Greater Lincolnshire.
 
A
draft proposal for a continued single tier of local government in
North Lincolnshire  was set out in
Appendix A (“the Proposal”) to the report.  It was considered appropriate that the three Upper
Tier Authorities in Lincolnshire, North Lincolnshire, North East
Lincolnshire and Lincolnshire County Council would individually set
out the preferred case for their own respective geographies, and
collectively their submissions would represent a single proposal
for the whole geography of Greater Lincolnshire, in response to the
invitation from the Secretary of State.
 
Resolved – (a) That the Proposal
contained at Appendix A of the Chief Executive’s report for
submission to Government by 28 November 2025 be approved, and (b)
that delegated authority be given to the Chief Executive to make
any final amendments to the Proposal before submission to
Government by 28 November 2025.
topline: The Leader Portfolio for Community Leadership, Skills, Steel and Heavy Industry has decided to approve the proposal for Local Government Reorganisation in Greater Lincolnshire.

5        ADOPTION OF
THE STATEMENT OF COMMUNITY INVOLVEMENT – The Director:
Communities submitted a report seeking approval to adopt the
Statement of Community Involvement as the basis for consultation
and community engagement in the preparation of the North
Lincolnshire Local Plan, other relevant planning policy documents
and the consideration of planning applications.
 
The
Statement of Community Involvement (SCI) was a statutory document
required by the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004. It
outlined how the council would involve the community and
organisations in producing planning documents, including the Local
Plan, neighbourhood plans, and the consideration of planning
applications and pre-application enquiries.
 
Legislation required Local Planning Authorities to review their
SCI at least once every five years to ensure that policies remained
up to date and effectively addressed the needs of the local
community. The council adopted its previous SCI on 20 August 2018.
Cabinet Member approval to publish the Draft SCI for consultation
was issued on the 16 May 2025 (minute 3 refers). Public
consultation was carried out between May and July 2025.
 
The
report presented the feedback received from the consultation on the
draft SCI, outlined any corresponding amendments to the document,
and recommended its adoption for use in the daily operations of the
planning service. Thirteen responses were received during the
consultation process; none of these required significant changes to
the SCI.
 
Resolved – That the Statement of
Community Involvement, as set out at Appendix 1 to the report, be
approved and adopted.
topline: The Environment and Strategy Cabinet Member has decided to adopt the Statement of Community Involvement for the North Lincolnshire Local Plan.

content:
6        NORTH
LINCOLNSHIRE LOCAL PLAN: LOCAL DEVELOPMENT SCHEME AUGUST 2025
– The Director: Communities submitted a report seeking
approval of a revised Local Development Scheme (LDS), which set out
the updated timetable and scope for the preparation of the Local
Plan and associated development plan documents.
 
Local Planning Authorities (LPAs) were required under Section 15
of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 , as amended by
the Localism Act 2011, to prepare and maintain an up-to-date LDS.
The LDS must be publicly available and outline the schedule for
producing development plan documents, including the Local
Plan.
 
The
LDS was a three-year timetable for producing development plan
documents including the Local Plan. The LDS set out when documents
would be produced, their purpose and expected consultation periods.
It also covered annual monitoring activities. The current LDS was
approved by the Environment and Strategy Cabinet Member on 7 March
2025 (minute 1 refers).
 
To
ensure the council complied with the requirement that all Local
Planning Authorities have an up-to-date LDS in place, a revised LDS
had been prepared. The revised LDS proposed a new timeline for the
Local Plan, with Regulation 18 consultation now scheduled for
Spring 2026 and Regulation 19 publication by Autumn 2026. The
updated LDS maintained the objective of submitting the Local Plan
under the current plan-making framework, in accordance with the
government’s deadline of December 2026.
 
The
reasons for delays in progressing the timetable outlined in the
March 2025 LDS included review and rescoping of evidence based on
revised National Planning Policy Framework (December 2024), an
increase in the local housing target from 386 dwellings to 647 per
annum, and National Development Management policies to be produced
by government had not yet been published which would impact on the
content of the Plan.
 
Resolved – (a) That the Local
Development Scheme be approved and brought into effect as from the
date of the decision, and (b) that the Local Development Scheme be
published on the council's website.
topline: The Environment and Strategy Cabinet Member has decided to approve a revised Local Development Scheme, setting a new timeline for the Local Plan to comply with government deadlines.

paper and card

In

Permission was sought and attained to procure 70,000 burgundy

content:
The corresponding report of the
following item (Minute 3 refers) contains exempt information as
defined in Paragraph 3 of Part 1 of Schedule 12A of the Local
Government Act 1972 (as amended).
 
3        PROCUREMENT
AND AWARD OF CONTRACT FOR SUPPLY OF 240L BURGUNDY RECYCLING
CONTAINERS – The Director: Communities submitted a report
seeking approval for the procurement of 70,000 240L burgundy
wheeled bin containers as part of the new Simpler Recycling
kerbside collections.
 
Introduced as part of the
Environment Act 2021, the new Simpler Recycling legislation for
domestic collections would come into effect from 1 April
2026.
 
The preferred new kerbside
collection methodology, to come into effect from 1 April
2026,  had now been identified and
received Cabinet Member approval (minute 1 refers).
 
The preferred collection
methodology included the necessary initial purchase of 70,000 240L
burgundy coloured wheeled bin containers and their ongoing supply
as part of the change to a fully co-mingled recycling kerbside
collection methodology.
 
Resolved
– That Option 1, as set out in the report at
paragraph 3.1 that the procurement of new 240L burgundy wheeled bin
containers, be approved.
topline: The Deputy Leader - Operations and Flooding Cabinet Member has decided to approve the procurement of 70,000 240L burgundy recycling containers for the new Simpler Recycling kerbside collections.
